Content: problems/AP14P2/media/1a.jpg
A proton is traveling to the left when it enters the space between `text(two)` oppositely charged parallel plates, as shown above. Which of the `text(four)` labeled paths will the proton take?

Key.Rationale: The electric field between the plates exerts a steady force directed up-the-page. Path `A` would result from the proton receiving a brief “jolt” toward the negative plate but then traveling freely with no forces exerted upon it.

The motion is analogous to a ball thrown sideways. The ball's horizontal velocity stays constant while the ball gains vertical velocity at a constant rate due to uniform gravitational field, leading to a curved trajectory. The same reasoning applies here, with the uniform electric field making the proton “fall” toward the upper plate.
The proton would follow this path only if no electric force were exerted on it, or if a down-the-page force canceled the up-the-page electric force.
The proton is positively charged and is therefore attracted to the upper plate and repelled from the lower `text(one)`.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/2a.jpg
problems/AP14P2/media/2b.jpg

The figures above represent `text(two)` fields. The figure on the left represents the uniform gravitational field very near `text(Earth's)` surface. The figure on the right represents the uniform electric field `E` near the center of the region between very large parallel plates. Which of the following describes the shape of the isolines of potential for the gravitational field and the electric field in these regions?

A.Choice: Isolines are straight, vertical lines for both the gravitational and electric fields.

Key.Rationale: The field vectors are vertical, but not the isolines. By definition, when an object travels along an isoline, the system neither gains nor loses potential energy. But the system loses potential energy when an object “falls” in the direction of the field.

B.Choice: Isolines are straight, horizontal lines for both the gravitational and electric fields.

Key.Rationale: By definition, when an object moves along an isoline, the system neither gains nor loses potential energy. Because the field vectors are purely vertical, the isolines must be purely horizontal. That way, an object moving along an isoline neither “rises” nor “falls” with respect to the field; in other words, the system neither gains nor loses potential energy.

C.Choice: Gravitational isolines are straight, while electric isolines are curved.

Key.Rationale: The electric isolines must be perpendicular to the electric field vectors at all points, or else a component of a charged object's motion along an isoline would be parallel to the field, causing a change in potential energy - which contradicts the definition of isoline. To be perpendicular to vertical field vectors, the isolines must be horizontal everywhere, which means they must be straight, not curved.

D.Choice: Gravitational isolines are curved, while electric isolines are straight.

Key.Rationale: This question is approximating the gravitational field as uniform near the `text(Earth's)` surface, which means the gravitational field vectors all point in the same direction.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/3a.jpg
The figure above shows a model of an electromagnetic wave, where `E` is the electric field and `B` is the magnetic field. In what direction is the energy of the wave transmitted?

Key.Rationale: Electromagnetic waves, like waves on a string, are transverse: the direction of the “disturbance” is perpendicular to the direction in which the waves travel, i.e., the direction in which energy is transmitted. Here, the electric and magnetic “disturbances” are `ytext(-directed)` and `ztext(-directed)`; therefore the waves must be traveling perpendicular to both of those transverse disturbances, along the `xtext(-axis)`.
A transverse wave moves and carries energy perpendicular to the direction of the “disturbance,” which here includes the `ytext(-directed)` electric disturbance.
A transverse wave moves and carries energy perpendicular to the direction of the “disturbance,” which here includes the `ztext(-directed)` magnetic disturbance.

D.Choice: In a direction that is at a `text(nonzero)` angle to each of the axes

Key.Rationale: A transverse wave transmits energy exactly perpendicular to the direction of the “disturbance,” which here means perpendicular to the `y` and `z` `text(axes)`. Only the `xtext(-axis)` satisfies this condition.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/4a.jpg

`text(Three)` identical conducting spheres, `S1`, `S2`, and `S3`, are supported by insulating thread, as shown above. Initially, sphere `S1` has a net positive charge and the other `text(two)` spheres are uncharged. Spheres `S1` and `S2` are brought into contact and then separated. Next, spheres `S2` and `S3` are brought into contact and then separated. Which of the following shows the signs of the final net charges on the spheres?

Key.Rationale: When `S2` touches `S1`, the electric potentials of the spheres equalize, which happens only if `S1` “shares” some of its excess positive charge with `S2`. (More precisely, electrons flow from `S2` to `S1`.) By the same reasoning, `S2` “shares” some of its excess charge with `S3` when they touch. So, all `text(three)` spheres end up positive.

If the spheres were non-conducting, then `S1` might “keep” all its excess positive charge. But the spheres are conductors. So, when `S1` touches `S2`, some “free” electrons on `S2`, attracted by the positive charge of `S1`, flow onto `S1`. This leaves `S2` with a net positive charge (i.e., an electron deficit). The same thing then happens when `S2` touches `S3`.

It would only occur if all the excess charge gets transferred when `text(each pair)` of spheres touch. When `S1` touches `S2`, their charges equalize instead of `S2` ending up with all the excess positive charge. That's because charge flows from `text(one)` sphere to the other until the spheres have the same electric potential, which for identical spheres means the charges equalize.
When `S1` touches `S2`, their charges equalize instead of `S2` ending up with all the excess positive charge.

Content: Which of the following correctly ranks the potential differences `DeltaV_1`, `DeltaV_2`, `DeltaV_3`, and `DeltaV_4` across the bulbs while the switch is open?

Key.Rationale: The current through a given bulb is `I=DeltaV_text(bulb)//r` where `DeltaV_text(bulb)` is the potential drop across that bulb. Therefore, equal potential drops across the bulbs would indicate equal currents. But bulb `1` has more current through it than the other bulbs do because the current “splits” before heading through bulb `2` or `3`.

Because the potential drop between `text(two)` points is path-independent, the potential drop across bulb `2` must equal the combined potential drop across `3` and `4`: `DeltaV_2=DeltaV_3_DeltaV_4`. Because these potential drops are `text(nonzero)`, `DeltaV_2` must be greater than, not equal to, `DeltaV_3`.

Because the current through a bulb is `I=DeltaV_text(bulb)//r`, where `DeltaV_text(bulb)` is the potential drop across that bulb, and because the resistances are all equal, it follows that the bulb with the greatest current is the bulb with the greatest `DeltaV_text(bulb)`. So, `DeltaV_1` is greatest. Similarly, because the same current flows through bulbs `3` and `4` in series, `DeltaV_3` must equal `DeltaV_4` . Because the potential drop between the `text(two)` junctions is path-independent, the potential drop across bulb `2` must equal the combined potential drop across `3` and `4`: `DeltaV_2=DeltaV_3_DeltaV_4`. Therefore, `DeltaV_2` must be greater than `DeltaV_3` and `DeltaV_4`.

It implies that some current gets “used up” in bulb `3`; however, all the current through `3` also flows through `4`. Because those currents are equal and those bulbs have equal resistance, the potential drops across `3` and `4` are equal.

Content: Immediately after the switch is closed, the current in bulb `1` is `I_a`. What is the current in bulb `2` at that time?

Key.Rationale: At the junction, `I_a` “splits,” with some flowing through bulb `2` and the rest flowing through bulb `3`. Therefore the current through bulb `2` is less than `I_a`.

This is the current through bulb `2` before the switch is closed, and also a long time after the switch is closed, when current no longer flows through the capacitor. But immediately after the switch is closed, the capacitor acts as short circuit providing a resistance-less path around bulb `4`.

Immediately after the switch is closed, the capacitor has no charge built up on it and therefore generates no potential difference. It therefore behaves like a resistance-less wire; all current through bulb `3` “sidesteps” bulb `4` and flows through the capacitor instead. At that time, the branch of the circuit containing bulbs `3` and `4` has `text(one)` bulb's worth of resistance instead of `text(two)` bulb's worth. The current through bulb `1` therefore splits equally between bulb `2` and bulb `3`.

At all times, the resistance of the branch containing bulbs `3` and `4` is the same or greater than the resistance of the branch containing bulb `2`. Therefore the current through bulb `2` is never less than `I_a//2`.

Content: After the switch has been closed a long time, how does the brightness of bulb `4` compare with its brightness before the switch was closed?

A.Choice: Bulb `4` is much dimmer and is only barely lit.

Key.Rationale: Once the capacitor reaches its “final” charge, current no it, and therefore all the current through bulb `3` also flows through bulb `4`. Therefore, significant current flows through bulb `4`.

While the capacitor is charging, current flows through the capacitor's segment of the circuit, “diverting” current away from bulb `4` and therefore dimming bulb `4`. Once the capacitor is “fully” charged, no current is diverted and hence bulb `4` is just as bright as before.

Once the capacitor reaches its “final” charge, current no longer flows through it - as was the case before the switch was closed. As a result, all the bulbs are exactly as bright as they were before the switch was closed.

Soon after the switch is closed, the short circuit around bulb `4` reduces the overall resistance of the circuit, and some of the bulbs get brighter (though not bulb `4`). A long time after the switch is closed, the capacitor is “fully” charged and hence a dead end to current; the circuit's overall resistance has returned to its value before the switch was closed.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/8a.jpg

A light ray enters a layer of water at point `X`, passes through a layer of glass, and exits through a layer of air at point `Y`, as shown in the figure above. Where would the ray exit the layer of air if the glass was replaced with a material of higher index of refraction?

Key.Rationale: By Snell's law, a higher index of refraction results in a smaller angle of transmission; the ray in the middle layer is closer to horizontal. The ray hits the middle-layer/air boundary above the point shown in the figure. For that reason, and also because the angle of transmission into the air is less than before (because the angle of incidence is less), the ray exits the air layer above point `Y`.

If the glass were replaced by a substance whose `n` were less than that of glass, the ray in the middle layer would be angled more sharply downward and would exit the air below `Y`. But increasing the `n` of the middle layer has the opposite effect.
Changing the index of refraction of the middle layer changes the path of the ray.

D.Choice: The location cannot be determined without knowing how much higher the index of refraction of the new material is.

Key.Rationale: Knowing the exact `n` would enable us to find exactly how far above `Y` the ray now exits the air. But Snell's law holds for any `n` greater than `n_text(glass)`.

Content: Which of the following indicates the object distance `s_o` for which a spherical concave mirror of focal length `f` produces an upright image?

Key.Rationale: By tracing rays and “backtracking” them to locate the virtual image behind the mirror, the student can confirm that the image is magnified and upright (unflipped).
This situation produces a blur because rays from the object reflect off the mirror parallel to one another, never converging or diverging to form an image.
By tracing rays, you can confirm that the image is magnified and inverted (flipped).
By tracing rays, you can confirm that the image is reduced in size and inverted (flipped).

Water is flowing with a speed of `9.0` `text(m)//text(s)` through a pipe of diameter `10` `text(cm)`. The pipe widens to `30` `text(cm)` as it goes up an `8.0` `text(m)` step, as shown in the figure above. If the pressure at point `A` is `2.0xx10^5` `text(Pa)` , what is the pressure at point `B`? (The density of water is `1.0xx10^3` `text(kg)//text(m)^3`.)

Key.Rationale: It could stem from taking into account the potential energy terms (`rhogh`) but not the kinetic energy terms, `(1//2)rhov`.

From the continuity equation (`A_1v_1=A_2v_2`), because the diameter of the pipe triples between `A` and `B`, its cross-sectional area increases by a factor of `9`, and hence the water's speed at `B` is `text(one ninth)` its speed at `A`, namely `1.0` `text(m)//text(s)`. From Bernoulli's equation, setting `y=0` in the lower pipe, we then get `2.0xx10^5` `text(Pa)+0+(1//2)(1.0xx10^3` `text(kg)//text(m)^3)(9.0` `text(m)//text(s))^2=P_B+(1.0xx10^3` `text(kg)//text(m)^3)(10` `text(m)//text(s)^2)(8.0` `text()m)+(1//2)(1.0xx10^3` `text(kg)//text(m)^3)(1.0` `text(m)//text(s))^2`. In solving for `P_2`, it saves time to neglect the last term on the right-hand side, which is smaller than the other terms, and divide everything through by the density of water, (`1.0xx10^3` `text(kg)//text(m)^3`).
It could stem from substituting the given pressure into the side of the equation describing point `B` and solving for the pressure at point `A`.

It could stem from the Bernoulli equation, having the water speeds reversed (`1.0` `text(m)//text(s)` at `A`, and `9.0` `text(m)//text(s)` at `B`), while also substituting the given pressure into the side of the equation describing point `B` and solving for the pressure at point `A`.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/11a.jpg

The figure above represents a portion of a blood vessel with circular cross sections. The segment on the left has diameter `1.6` `text(mm)`, and each of the segments on the right has diameter `0.4` `text(mm)`. Assume the blood can be treated as an ideal fluid. If blood enters the segment on the left with speed `v`, at what speed does the blood leave the segments on the right?

Key.Rationale: By confusing diameter with area, `text(one)` would therefore think that the total exit diameter is `text(half)` that of the entry diameter, which would require an exit velocity `text(twice)` that of the entry velocity.
Confusing diameter with area, and comparing the entry of the exit diameters gives a `4` to `1` ratio of entry to exit diameter which requires `4` times the entry velocity.

The area through which fluid enters is `8` times the area through which fluid leaves. The volume entering `text(each second)` must equal the volume leaving `text(each second)` so the fluid must leave at `text(eight)` times the rate it enters.
By comparing entry area with only `text(one)` of the exit areas `text(one)` would obtain a `16` to `1` ratio of areas, requiring `16` times the entry velocity.

Content: A slab of metal and a slab of wood are placed in a classroom and allowed to sit undisturbed for a long time. A student then places `text(one)` hand on the metal and the other hand on the wood. Which of the following describes the student's perception of the temperatures of the slabs and their actual temperatures?

A.Choice: The metal slab feels colder to the student because it is at a lower temperature.

Key.Rationale: The slabs are in thermal equilibrium with the room, so both are at room temperature.

B.Choice: The metal slab feels colder to the student because it conducts thermal energy away from the student's hand faster, but the slabs have the same temperature.

Key.Rationale: The slabs are in thermal equilibrium with the room and at the same temperature, but perception of temperature depends on the rate of thermal energy transfer. Metal has higher thermal conductivity than wood, so it feels colder when touched by the warmer hand of the student.

C.Choice: The metal slab feels warmer to the student because it conducts thermal energy to the student's hand faster, but the slabs have the same temperature.

Key.Rationale: If room temperature were hotter than body temperature, the metal slab would feel warmer due to a higher rate of thermal energy transfer.

D.Choice: Both slabs feel the same to the student because they are at the same temperature.

Key.Rationale: Although the slabs are at the same temperature, the perception of temperature depends on the rate of heat transfer to the materials and the metal slab has higher thermal conductivity.

Content: When `text(one)` end of a cold metal spoon is placed upright in a cup of hot cocoa, the other end eventually gets warmer. On the scale of the molecules of the spoon, which of the following is the primary explanation of this phenomenon?

A.Choice: Higher-energy molecules will, on average, rise to the top.

Key.Rationale: Thermal convection in a fluid can be confused with thermal conduction in the solid spoon.

B.Choice: The hot molecules produce thermal radiation that is then absorbed by the colder molecules.

Key.Rationale: Thermal radiation will transfer some thermal energy, but in the solid spoon this process would not be the primary process for thermal energy transfer.

C.Choice: Higher-energy molecules hit lower-energy molecules and, on average, tend to reduce the difference in temperature between the ends of the spoon.

Key.Rationale: At the molecular scale, higher temperature means higher kinetic energy and momentum of molecules. Collisions between higher momentum and lower momentum molecules will tend to transfer momentum and kinetic energy from higher momentum molecules to the lower momentum `text(ones)`. This results in energy transfer from the hotter regions to the cooler regions of the spoon until the material reaches thermal equilibrium.

D.Choice: Thermal energy is a fluid that flows from high concentration (hot areas) to low concentration (cold areas).

Key.Rationale: Historically a fluid flow analogy for thermal energy transfer reflected the idea that 'heat' was a substance that could flow from place to place.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/14a.jpg

An object with charge `+q` passes to the right of `text(one)` pole of a magnet and at a particular instant is moving with a velocity `vecv` toward the bottom of the page, as shown in the figure above. The force exerted on the object by the magnet at that instant is directed into the page. What is the direction of the force exerted on the magnet by the object?

Key.Rationale: The force exerted on the moving charged object by the magnet and the force exerted on the magnet by the moving charged object are an interaction described by Newton's `text(third)` law and have equal magnitudes and opposite directions.

The forces exerted in the interaction must be in opposite directions. Thinking about a magnet as attracting an object such as a small piece of steel, `text(one)` would reason that the `text(third)` law force would therefore attract the magnet to the right.

C.Choice: Toward the top of the page

Key.Rationale: The forces exerted in the interaction must be in opposite directions.

All forces are interactions described by Newton's `text(third)` law, therefore if there is a force exerted on the moving charged object by the magnet there must be a force exerted on the magnet by the moving charged object.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/15a.jpg

A student was given `text(five)` wires of the same length and diameter. The student connected the wires to the same battery `text(one)` by `text(one)` and measured the current through `text(each wire)`. The table above shows the data collected. Which of the following can be concluded from the data?

Key.Rationale: To determine if a wire is ohmic would require a data set of current measurements for different potential differences for a `text(single)` wire.

B.Choice: The wires are made of different materials.

Key.Rationale: The resistance of a wire is determined by the length, cross-sectional area and resistivity of the material. Because the lengths and diameters are the same, and the same battery is used with `text(each wire)`, the materials must be different in order for there to be different resistances resulting in different currents.

C.Choice: The resistance of the wires depends on their size and shape.

Key.Rationale: The resistance of the wires does depend on the size and shape, but also on the material. Because the size and shape of all the wires are the same, this would not account for the different resistance.

If the wires have different resistances, any internal resistance of the battery would mean different terminal voltages, but without measuring the voltage across the wires, no conclusion can be made about the internal resistance of the battery.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/16a.jpg

In the figure above, the initially uncharged insulating rod on the left is free to rotate on an insulating stand. End `X` is then rubbed with a piece of fur. End `Z` of a `text(second)` insulating rod is also rubbed with fur and then brought near the `text(first)` rod. As the `text(second)` rod is moved around, it is found that end `Y` of the `text(first)` rod is attracted to end `Z`, and end `X` is repelled. Which of the following correctly describes the signs of the charges on ends `X` and `Y`, if any?

A.Choice:
`ultext(End X)`: Opposite `text(Z's)` charge
`ultext(End Y)`: Same as `text(Z's)` charge

Key.Rationale: Because `X` and `Z` repel, they must have net charges of the same sign. If `Y` had a net charge of the same sign as `Z` it would also be repelled by `Z`.

B.Choice:
`ultext(End X)`: Opposite `text(Z's)` charge
`ultext(End Y)`: No net charge

Key.Rationale: Because `X` and `Z` repel, they must have net charges of the same sign.

C.Choice:
`ultext(End X)`: Same as `text(Z's)` charge
`ultext(End Y)`: Opposite `text(Z's)` charge

Key.Rationale: `X` and `Z` have the same charge due to transfer of electrons between the rods and the fur, not motion of charges along the rods. No charging process occurred with end `Y` to give it a net charge.

D.Choice:
`ultext(End X)`: Same as `text(Z's)` charge
`ultext(End Y)`: No net charge

Key.Rationale: Because ends `X` and `Z` are the same materials and were rubbed with the same fur, they will have the same sign of charge and will repel each other. End `Y` was not rubbed, will have no net charge and is attracted to end `Z` by the polarization induced by the presence of end `Z`.

Content: A student has a positively charged insulating rod and `text(two)` initially uncharged conducting spheres, `A` and `B`, with insulated handles. Which of the following ordered sequences of actions could the student use to produce a net positive charge on sphere `A`?

A.Choice: Bring the rod near the right side of `A`. Touch `B` to the left side of `A`. Remove `B` and then remove the rod.

Key.Rationale: The positive rod attracts electrons to the right side of `A` leaving the left side positively charged. Touching `B` to `A` allows electrons from `B` to move to the left side of A until the left side of `A` is neutral. When `B` is removed it will have lost electrons to `A`, which will therefore have a net negative charge.

B.Choice: Bring the rod near the right side of `A`. Touch `B` to the left side of `A`. Remove the rod and then remove `B`.

Key.Rationale: Removing the rod before breaking the connection between `B` and `A` allows electrons that moved from `B` to `A` to return to `B`, therefore both `B` and `A` will have no net charge.

C.Choice: Bring the rod near the right side of `B`. Touch `A` to the left side of `B`. Remove `B` and then remove the rod.

Key.Rationale: The positive rod attracts electrons to the right side of `B` leaving the left side positively charged. Touching `A` to `B` allows electrons from `A` to move to the left side of `B`. When `B` is removed from `A`, `A` is left with a net positive charge, which is the desired outcome.

D.Choice: Bring the rod near the right side of `B`. Touch `A` to the left side of `B`. Remove the rod and then remove `B`.

Key.Rationale: Removing the rod before separating the spheres results in both spheres ending with no net charge.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/18a.jpg

The figure above shows a long conducting wire that lies in the plane of the page and carries an electric current `I` toward the right. At the instant shown, a positive point charge `+q` is in the plane of the page and moving toward the bottom of the page. What is the direction of the magnetic force on the point charge at that instant?

Key.Rationale: The magnetic field due to the electric current is directed into the page at the location of the charged object. The force exerted by the field on the charged object must be perpendicular to the magnetic field vector, not parallel to it.

The magnetic field due to the electric current is directed into the page at the location of the charged object. The force exerted by the field on the charged object must be perpendicular to the magnetic field vector, not anti-parallel to it.

The magnetic field due to the electric current is directed into the page at the location of the charged object. The force exerted on the moving charge by the field is perpendicular to both the field vector and the velocity vector and for a positive charge is directed to the right.
A mistake in determining the direction of the magnetic field or applying the right-hand rule for the field's effect on the point charge could give this option.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/19a.jpg

The figure above shows `text(three)` point charges located on an `xtext(-axis)`. Which of the following ranks the magnitude of the net electric force, `F`, on `text(each point)` charge due to the other charges?

Key.Rationale: Assuming force to the right is positive, the net force on `A` is `-4kQ^2//9+2kQ^2//1`. The net force on `B` is `8kQ^2//4-2kQ^2//1` and the net force on `C` is `-8kQ^2//4+4kQ^2//9`. The question asks for magnitude of net force, so `F_A=F_C=abs(2kQ^2//1-rkQ^2//9)` and `F_B=0`.

The `text(two)` outside point charges exert forces in opposite directions and of equal magnitude on the point charge `B`, therefore the net force on `B` is `text(zero)` and it cannot be the greatest in magnitude.

This answer choice has the magnitude of force on `B` greater than the force on `C`, which cannot be true. The `text(two)` outside point charges exert forces in opposite directions and of equal magnitude on the point charge; therefore the net force on `B` is `text(zero)`.

If the force to the right is considered to be positive, then the net force on `A` is `-4kQ^2//9+2kQ^2//1`.  The net force on `B` is `8kQ^2//4-2kQ^2//1` and the net force on `C` is `-8kQ^2//4+4kQ^2//9`. Because the net force on `A` is equal to the net force on `C`, this answer choice cannot be true.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/20a.jpg

A block is submerged in a container of liquid and held under the surface of the liquid by a string connected to the bottom of the container, as shown in the figure above. The tension in the string is not `text(zero)`. How does the buoyant force `F_B` exerted by the liquid on the block compare to the block's weight `w`?

Key.Rationale: Because the tension and weight are both downward, the weight cannot be greater than the buoyant force, as this would leave the tension with a negative value.

The block is in static equilibrium, so the net force on the block is `text(zero)`. Because there are `text(three)` vertical forces on the block - the buoyant force, the weight, and the tension, no `text(two)` of those forces in opposite directions could be equal to each other.

Because the block is in static equilibrium, the net force on the block is `text(zero)`. Net force is the vector sum of buoyant force upward and both tension and weight downward. Therefore, the buoyant force has to be greater than either of the individual downward forces.

D.Choice: Either `F_B<w` or `F_B>w`, depending on the density of the liquid.

Key.Rationale: Changing the density of the liquid does change the buoyant force, but a buoyant force is still exerted on the block. Because the block is in static equilibrium, the net force on the block is `text(zero)`. Net force is the vector sum of buoyant force upward and both tension and weight downward. Therefore, the buoyant force has to be greater than either of the individual downward forces.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/21a.jpg

A variable resistor is connected to a battery of unknown potential difference. The power dissipated by the resistor and the current through the resistor are measured. The figure above shows a graph of the data and a best-fit line for the data. The potential difference provided by the battery is most nearly

Key.Rationale: The slope of the graph should be equal to the potential difference becase `P=VI`, but this value, `0.3` `text(V)`, is not a correct calculation of the slope.

This choice is the area under the graph line at the point `(1,6)`, but the area of a power vs. current graph does not give you the potential difference. It could also be an incorrect calculation of the slope between `text(two)` data points that are not on the line.
This choice represents an incorrect calculation of slope, using `text(two)` data points that are not on the best fit line.

Electrical power is equal to the product of potential difference and current (`P=VI`). A graph of power as a function of current has potential difference as its slope. Using any `text(two)` points on the best-fit line (such as `1,6` and `0,0`), the slope is `6.0` `text(W)//text(A)` or `6.0` `text(V)`.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/22a.jpg
:ibox:`ultext(Note)`: Figure not drawn to scale.

A scientist is studying the radioactive decay of an element and wants to determine the sign of some of the particles emitted. The scientist lets a beam of the particles, all with the same speed, pass through an opening in a shield and enter the field created by a wire carrying a constant current. Paths `1` and `2` represent the observed paths of the particles. Based on the paths, which of the following could be the types of particles?

Key.Rationale: An electron is negative and an alpha is positive, so they would curve in opposite directions in the magnetic field (according to the right hand rule) - not in the same direction as shown in the diagram.
An electron is negative and an alpha is positive, so they would curve in opposite directions in a magnetic field - not the same direction.

Using a right hand rule to determine force exerted on a charged particle moving in a magnetic field, the force is in the same direction on both particles only if they have the same type of charge. Setting the expression for centripetal force equal to magnetic force, the radius of curvature is equal to `mv//qB`. Both the alpha and positron are positive, but the alpha has `text(twice)` the charge and `text(four)` times the mass, so the alpha takes path `2` with a larger radius.

Both the alpha and positron are positive, but the alpha has `text(twice)` the charge and `text(four)` times the mass. This answer choice incorrectly has the particle with smaller mass-to-charge ratio taking the path of larger radius.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/23a.jpg

The energy states for an electron in a hypothetical atom are represented above. A cold sample of gas of such atoms is illuminated by a brief flash of light with a continuous spectrum. The atoms are then observed to emit light with discrete wavelengths. Which of the following transitions produces the longest wavelength light?

Key.Rationale: The `n=5` to `n=4` transition selected here does not have the smallest spacing and therefore does not have the smallest energy and longest wavelength.

The longest wavelength light has the lowest frequency (`c=flambda`) and thus the lowest energy (`E=hf`). On this diagram, lower energy transitions are shown with smaller spacing between lines. The `n=4` to `n=3` transition has the smallest spacing and thus smallest energy and longest wavelength.
The `n=3` to `n=2` transition does not have the smallest spacing and thus does not have the smallest energy and longest wavelength.
The `n=2` to `n=1` transition selected here has the largest spacing and thus would have the largest energy and shortest wavelength - not the longest wavelength.

Content: A nucleus of `text()_92^238text(Pb)` undergoes a series of decays in which it emits `text(eight)` `text()_2^4text(He)` nuclei and some `beta^-` particles to produce the nucleus `text()_82^206text(Pb)`. How many `beta^-` particles are emitted in the process?

Key.Rationale: The `text(eight)` heliums (`text(H3)`) produced account for `16` positive charges, so the emission of `10` negative charges (`beta^-`) leaves an imbalance of `4` negative. This answer choice does not conserve charge.
The `text(eight)` heliums (`text(He)`) produced account for `16` positive charges, so the emission of `8` negative charges (`beta^-`) leaves an imbalance of `2` negative and charge is not conserved.

Because beta particles do not have mass number, conservation of charge is used to balance the reaction. The change in atomic number from the element uranium (`text(U)`) to lead (`text(Pb)`) is a reduction of `10` positive charges. The `text(eight)` heliums (`text(He)`) account for production of `16` positive charges, so there needs to be `6` negative charges (`beta^-`) emitted also for a net change of `text(zero)`.
The `text(eight)` heliums (`text(He)`) produced account for `16` positive charges, so the emission of `5` negative charges (`beta^-`) leaves an imbalance of `1` positive and charge is not conserved.

The graph above shows the wave function `Psi(x)` of a particle moving in the region `0<x<4` `text(m)`. At which of the following positions is the probability of finding the particle greatest?

Key.Rationale: The amplitude at `x=0.7` `text(m)` is about `1`, so `Psi^2=1`, which is not the greatest value among the answer choices.

The greatest probability of locating the wave is at a position along the `xtext(-axis)` where the magnitude of the amplitude is the greatest, or where `Psi^2` has the greatest value. This occurs at `x=2.0` `text(m)`, where the magnitude of `Psi` is `3` and `Psi^2` is `9`.
The amplitude at `x=2.5` `text(m)` is about `1.5`, so `Psi^2` does not have the greatest value among the answer choices.
The amplitude at `x=4.0` `text(m)` is `text(zero)`, so this answer choice represents the smallest probability among the answer choices given - not the largest.

Content: The focal length of the lens is approximately

Key.Rationale: Start with the thin lens equation, `1//f=1//s_o +1//s_i` and rearrange the terms to show reciprocal of image distance as a function of reciprocal of object distance, as in the graph: `1//s_i=-1//s_o +1//f`. In this `y=mx+b` form, it's clear that the slope is `-1` and the `ytext(-intercept)` is equal to the reciprocal of the focal length. The `ytext(-intercept)` is `2.0`, so the focal length is `0.5` `text(m)`.
The value `1.0` is the magnitude of the slope, which would be `-s_o//s_i` and is not a correct calculation of focal length.
The `ytext(-intercept)` is `2.0`. This answer choice does not take the reciprocal of the intercept to correctly determine the focal length.
The `ytext(-intercept)` is `2.0`, so the focal length is `0.5` `text(m)`. This answer choice may represent the product of the `x` and `y` `text(intercepts)`, which is not a correct calculation.

Content: What is the magnitude of the image's magnification when the object is placed `2` `text(m)` from the lens?

Key.Rationale: Magnification is the absolute value of the ratio of image height to object height, which is the same ratio as image distance to object distance (`s_i//s_o`). When `s_i=2` `text(m)`, `1//s_i` is `0.5`, which corresponds to (`1//s_o`) equal to `1.5`. Then `s_o` equals `2//3` and the magnification is `1//3`.
This is a calculation of the magnitude of the slope of the line, but the slope of this graph does not give you the magnification.
Magnification is the absolute value of the ratio of image height to object height, but this answer choice incorrectly calculates the ratio of object height to image height.

D.Choice: The magnification is undefined because the image is an infinite distance from the lens.

Key.Rationale: It could be chosen if `text(one)` looked at the value of the image distance (`2` `text(m)`) instead of its reciprocal.

Content: A partially evacuated vertical cylindrical container is covered by a circular lid that makes an airtight seal. The pressure in the room surrounding the container is `1.01xx10^5` `text(N)//text(m)^2`, and the pressure inside the container is `0.41xx10^5` `text(N)//text(m)^2` . The lid has radius `0.20` `text(m)` and weight `200` `text(N)`. The minimum upward applied force required to lift the lid is most nearly

Key.Rationale: This choice omits the force that accounts for the weight of the lid.

The minimum upward force is equal to the net downward force on the lid, which is the sum of the weight of the lid and the net downward force  due to air. The pressure outside is greater than pressure inside, so net pressure times the area of the lid is net force due to air. `sumF_text(up)=sumF_text(down)=(1.01xx10^5-0.40xx10^5)(pir^2)+200` `text(N)=7.7xx10^3` `text(N)`.
The calculation for this option incorrectly used only the outside pressure and has omitted the pressure of the gas inside, using only `1.01xx10^5` times the area.
This option incorrectly added the pressures inside and outside the container instead of subtracting them.

Content: A sealed container of air has been sitting on a table in a dark room for a very long time. The room is always kept at a constant temperature. Which of the following best describes what will happen to the speeds and the average kinetic energy of the molecules of the air in the container as the container continues to sit on the table?

A.Choice: `text(Each molecule)` will continue to move at constant speed, keeping the average kinetic energy of the molecules constant.

Key.Rationale: Constant temperature indicates a constant average kinetic energy, but speeds of individual molecules will vary. This answer choice has incorrectly assumed that molecular speeds must stay constant if temperature is constant

B.Choice: Some molecules will speed up and others will slow down, keeping the average kinetic energy of the molecules constant.

Key.Rationale: If the room temperature is constant and the container and air are in equilibrium, the average translational kinetic energy of molecules remains constant. However, speeds of individual molecules will vary due to collisions between them.

C.Choice: The molecules will gradually slow down, decreasing their average kinetic energy.

Key.Rationale: The statement comes from an assumption that the molecules will lose kinetic energy as the container sits, but for that to be true the temperature would have to decrease. If the room is kept at constant temperature, the container should remain in equilibrium and at constant temperature.

D.Choice: The molecules will gradually speed up, increasing their average kinetic energy.

Key.Rationale: This answer choice is impossible in a situation where temperature remains constant and the room and container are in equilibrium. The average kinetic energy would increase only if temperature increased.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/31a.jpg

The figure above shows a long, straight wire that has a steady current `I` in the `+ytext(-direction)`. A small object with charge `+q` hangs from a thread near the wire. A student wants to investigate the magnetic force on the object due to the current but is not able to observe or measure changes in the tension in the string. Of the following actions that the student can take, which will allow the student to observe a reaction of the object due to the magnetic force on it?

Key.Rationale: Using a right hand rule and `F_B=qv_|_B`, holding the object motionless would not produce any magnetic force, because `v=0`.

B.Choice: Moving the object in a circle that is centered on the wire and in the `xtext(-)z` `text(plane)`

Key.Rationale: Using a right hand rule, the magnetic field lines are circles centered on the wire. Moving the object in a circle in the `xtext(-)z` `text(plane)` means it is moving along a field line, so the velocity is always parallel to the field. Using `F_B=qv_|_B`, there is no magnetic force.

Moving the object in the `-x` `text(direction)` will produce a magnetic force on the object in the `-y` `text(direction)`, changing the tension in the string, which the students will not be able to observe directly.

With the direction of current given, using a right hand rule, the magnetic field near the small object is directed into the page (in the `-z` `text(direction)`). Using a right hand rule and `F_B=qv_|_B`, moving the object in the `+y` `text(direction)` will produce a magnetic force on the object in the `-x` `text(direction)`, which the students should be able to observe.

Content: A small positive test charge is held at point `P`. Which of the following is closest to the direction of the force exerted on the test charge?

Key.Rationale: Its direction is too far toward the left to be aligned with the electric field vectors, which are directed more to the upper left on the diagram.

The electric force on a positive charge is in the same direction as the electric field (`vecF=qvecE`). At point `P`, the field vectors are directed toward the top of the page and to the left, but not too extremely in either of those directions, so the force is in the same direction.

The direction of electric force indicated by the answer choice would be correct only if the point `P` were moved to the right in the diagram. The force vector shown is not aligned with the electric field at point `P`.

The electric force vector shown is not aligned with the electric field at point `P`. This force vector would only be correct if the point `P` were moved to the right and slightly below the point charge.

Content: Which of the following indicates the particles with charges of the greatest and the least magnitude?

Key.Rationale: Particles `2` and `4` have a magnitude intermediate between that of `1` and `3`.
The clear area representing electric field vectors of largest magnitude is largest for particle `1` and smallest for particle `3`, so this answer choice has the correct answer reversed.
Particles `2` and `4` have a magnitude intermediate between that of `1` and `3`.

Vectors with largest magnitude are not shown, so the blank areas represent regions with larger magnitude of electric field. Since the field is proportional to `q//r^2`, a larger blank area corresponds to a larger charge. The area is largest for particle `1` and smallest for particle `3`.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/34a.jpg

A parallel-plate capacitor is connected to a battery. A thick metal plate is located between the plates of the capacitor, as shown above. Which of the following best shows the distribution of charge on the thick plate?

Key.Rationale: The longer line (upper) on the battery connection higher potential (considered positive). Thus, conventional current will flow counterclockwise in the external circuit, making the upper plate of the capacitor positive and bottom plate negative. The thick plate in the middle will have opposite charges induced by the charged plates so that it essentially creates `text(two)` capacitors in series. Because of fringe effects near the ends of the thick plate the charges will move a little closer, creating the distribution as shown.
The diagram for this answer choice has incorrectly reversed the charges on the thick metal plate.
This answer choice has incorrectly ignored the fringe effects. Charges will move a little closer near the ends of the plates.
The diagram for this answer choice has incorrectly reversed the signs of charges on the inner plate and also has neglected fringe effects.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/35a.jpg

At the instant shown above, an electron is moving to the right along a straight line midway between `text(two)` identical bar magnets. Which of the following describes the path of the electron as it continues to move?

A.Choice: It remains on the straight line and passes completely between the magnets.

Key.Rationale: In this view, the field lines from each bar magnet exit the N pole and loop around to enter the S pole. Since the bar magnets are identical, when they are placed as shown the components of the field that do `ultext(not)` point from left to right tend to cancel. Midway between the magnets, the field is exactly from left to right. A charged particle (positive or negative) would be moving along the field lines - not crossing them - so no magnetic force would be exerted on the particle.

B.Choice: It curves upward and strikes the top magnet.

Key.Rationale: The particle would only curve upward on the diagram if there were a net magnet field directed out of the page. In this symmetrical situation with identical magnets, that would not be true.

C.Choice: It curves downward and reverses direction before it enters the space between the magnets.

Key.Rationale: The electron would only curve downward on the page if there were a net magnetic field directed into the page in the space between the magnets. The bar magnets are identical, so there is no net field into the page.

D.Choice: It stops and reverses direction, then moves to the left along the same straight line.

Key.Rationale: The electron would not stop and reverse direction unless there was a magnetic force directed to the left on the electron as it moves to the right. Using the right hand rule, there could be no magnetic force in line with the direction of motion of the electron.

Content: Which of the following procedures can a student follow to give a metallic sphere a positive charge by induction?

A.Choice: Touching the sphere with a positively charged rod

Key.Rationale: Touching the sphere constitutes a “conduction method”, not an “induction method”.

B.Choice: Placing a negatively charged rod near the sphere

Key.Rationale: Bringing the negatively charged object near the sphere is the initial step of induction, but it is not sufficient. This polarizes the sphere, but does not leave the sphere with a new net charge.

C.Choice: Placing a positively charged rod near the sphere, grounding the sphere, and then removing the connection to ground

Key.Rationale: This option correctly describes an induction process, but it would leave the metallic sphere charged negatively after the process.

D.Choice: Placing a negatively charged rod near the sphere, grounding the sphere, and then removing the connection to ground

Key.Rationale: The choice includes all of the necessary components for successfully inducing a charge. Bring a negatively charged object (opposite sign) close to a metal object. The charges on the sphere become polarized. The grounding allows the negative charges on the polarized sphere a pathway to leave the sphere, leaving the sphere positively charged. The interruption of the ground ensures the negative charge cannot return to the sphere, leaving the sphere a net positive charge.

Content: What is the current through the `40` `Omega` resistor?

Key.Rationale: `7.5` `text(mA)` is not a valid current value for any part of this circuit.

The `40` `text(ohm)` resistor and the ammeter are located in equivalent positions in the circuit. No matter what the direction of current through the ammeter, it will split at `text(one)` of the junctions on either side of the ammeter, and recombine when it reaches the corresponding junction on either side of the `40` `text(ohm)` resistor. So the `40` `text(ohm)` resistor also has a current of `20` `text(mA)`.
A current of `40` `text(mA)` is larger than the measured `20` `text(mA)` through the ammeter. This would violate the principle of conservation of charge.

Content: The resistance of resistor `R` is most nearly

Key.Rationale: It is the equivalent resistance of the section of the circuit to the right of `R`. A `50` `text(ohm)` resistor would lead to a net resistance of `25` `text(ohms)` for this entire right section of the circuit that includes `R`. This value would not result in equal division of the potential difference.

The voltage across the parallel multi branch section to the right of resistor `R` is `1.0` `text(Volt)`, the same as the measurement on the voltmeter. Since the `text(two)` `20` `text(ohm)` resistors are in equivalent positions, they share equally the remaining `2` `text(volts)` supplied by the battery. This means that the net resistance of the rest of the circuit must also be `20` `text(ohms)`. The equivalent resistance of the section of the circuit to the right of `R` is `50` `text(ohms)` - added in “parallel” to the unknown resistor must give `20` `text(ohms)`. The value that will give `20` `text(ohms)` is `33.3` `text(ohms)` {i.e., `(1//33.3)+(1//50)=1//20`}.

It may come from realizing that the given `20` `text(ohm)` resistors share the remaining `2` `text(volts)` potential difference, that is have `1` `text(volt)` each, and assuming that `R` must equal them to also have `1` `text(volt)`. A resistance of `20` `text(ohms)` would yield a net resistance of `14` `text(ohms)` for the entire right section of the circuit that includes `R`. This value would not result in the correct equal division of the potential difference .

A value of `14` `text(ohms)` yields a net resistance of `11` `text(ohms)` for the entire right section of the circuit that includes `R`. This value would not result in the correct equal division of the potential difference.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/39a.jpg

The figure above represents a section of a circuit containing `text(three)` resistors, `X`, `Y`, and `Z`, of different sizes but made of the same material. Which of the following correctly ranks the current in the resistors?

Key.Rationale: This choice follows in order of the resistances of the conductors.
This choice is ranking the lengths of the conductors.
There are clearly different lengths and areas. This would not lead to identical currents for these `text(three)` conductors.

Current is proportional to the cross sectional area of the conductor and inversely proportional to length of the conductor. Conductors `X` and `Y` have the same cross sectional area and `Y` has clearly the smaller length. Conductors `X` and `Z` have the same length, but `X` has a larger cross sectional area. This leads to the conclusion that `I_Y>I_X>I_Z`.

Content: `text(Three)` identical, small cork spheres are released from rest in a uniform electric field directed downward toward the floor. Sphere `X` is uncharged, but spheres `Y` and `Z` are charged. Sphere `Z` remains suspended in the field. Spheres `X` and `Y` fall downward, but sphere `X` takes a longer time to reach the floor. What are the signs of the charges on spheres `Y` and `Z`?

Key.Rationale: Evidence to support sphere `Y` being a negative charge would either be suspended (like sphere `Z`), or drifting upward. If sphere `Y` did move downward (with a negative charge), it would fall “slower” than sphere `X`.
Sphere `Z` could not be in a suspended state with a positive charge. A positive charge would give the sphere `text(two)` downward forces acting on it - and therefore no way for it to be suspended.
The choice of sphere `Z` being positive implies this  choice is incorrect.

Because the field is directed downward, the sphere `Z` must have a negative charge to be in suspended state (upward `F_E` and a downward weight vector). Sphere `Y` falls “faster” than the uncharged sphere, this makes sense if it has a positive charge. This results in `text(two)` downward forces (gravitational plus electrostatic) and a resultant downward force greater than the neutral sphere, thus falling “faster”.

Content: `text(Two)` charged objects are held at a distance `d` apart. Their mutual gravitational force is equal to their mutual electrostatic force. Which of the following must be true of the charges and masses of the objects, if charge is expressed in `C` and mass is expressed in `text(kg)`?

A.Choice: The magnitude of the product of the charges must equal the magnitude of the product of the masses.

Key.Rationale: The products of the charges cannot equal the products of the masses - this would not be a dimensionally correct comparison. It ignores the fact that the size of the physical constants `G` and `k` must be considered.

B.Choice: The magnitude of the product of the charges must be much less than the magnitude of the product of the masses.

Key.Rationale: The ratio of charge products to mass products is equivalent to `G//k` (which is approximately `10^-20`). This implies that the products of the charges are much, much less than the products of the masses.

C.Choice: The magnitude of the product of the charges must be much greater than the magnitude of the product of the masses.

Key.Rationale: This option is the inverse of the correct relationship.

D.Choice: The charges must be equal and the masses must be equal.

Key.Rationale: The masses being equal or the charges being equal does not allow for a comparison of the `text(two)` types of forces (gravitational versus electrostatic). The actual value of the masses or charges would need to be known to make a comparison.

When a constant current `I` in the indicated direction is created in the coils, the electron beam is deflected toward which edge of the screen?

Content: An absorption spectrum, observed for light traveling through interstellar gases, appears as a broad spectrum of light with isolated dark lines at frequencies characteristic of the molecules in the gases. Which of the following is primarily responsible for the location of the dark absorption lines in the spectrum?

A.Choice: The characteristic velocities of the molecules in the gas

Key.Rationale: The velocities of the gas molecules are directly related to the kinetic energy of the gas molecules (which relates to temperature of the gas). The speeds have no relation to the absorption spectrum.

B.Choice: The transition of electrons between discrete energy states within the gas molecules

Key.Rationale: The “location” of the dark lines is directly related to the color (and associated energy of that wavelength) of the light absorbed by the gas. This energy of this particular color is directly related to the transition of the electrons or the different “energy levels” in this particular gas.

C.Choice: The `text(percent)` of the gas molecules that were ionized by absorption of energy

Key.Rationale: The `text(percent)` of gas ionized would relate more closely to the relative absence of color from the spectrum (brightness/darkness) but not to the “location” of the dark spot in the spectrum.

D.Choice: The fluctuations in density of molecules present in the interstellar gas cloud

Key.Rationale: The fluctuation of density might affect how many molecules get ionized, but not where the spectrum's dark spots are located.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/44a.jpg

A student performs an experiment to determine the index of refraction of a plastic block. The student shines a laser beam from air (`n_text(air)=1`) into a piece of plastic (`n_text(plastic)`) at an angle of incidence `theta_1` and measures the angle of refraction `theta_2`, as shown in Figure `1` above. Measurements are taken as `theta_1` is increased. From the data the student produces the `text(two)` graphs shown below.
problems/AP14P2/media/44b.jpg
problems/AP14P2/media/44c.jpg
Which of the following is equal to the index of refraction of the plastic block?

A.Choice: The slope of the best-fit line for graph `1`

Key.Rationale: Graph `1` is clearly not a linear relationship and therefore does not have a best-fit line from which a slope can be extracted.

B.Choice: The slope of the best-fit line for graph `2`

Key.Rationale: Snell's law does give a linear relationship between the sine of the incident angle and the sine of the refracted angle, but the slope of this data is a value less than `text(one)` - and indices of refraction of common materials are greater than `text(one)`.

C.Choice: The inverse of the slope of the best-fit line for graph `1`

Key.Rationale: Graph `1` is clearly not a linear relationship and therefore does not have a best-fit line from which a slope can be extracted.

D.Choice: The inverse of the slope of the best-fit line for graph `2`

Key.Rationale: Snell's law yields a linear relationship between the sine of incident  angle and the sine of the refracted angle - in this case `n_text(air)sintheta_1=n_text(plastic)sintheta_2`. So the index of the plastic is the inverse of the slope. `text(One)` can also note that the slope of this graph is approximately `0.7`, and since the indices of common materials are greater than `1` the refractive index must be the inverse of slope.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/45a.jpg

In the circuit represented above, `text(two)` resistors (`R_1` and `R_2`), a capacitor `C`, and an open switch `S` are connected to a battery. The circuit reaches equilibrium. The switch is then closed, and the circuit is allowed to come to a new equilibrium. Which of the following is a true statement about the energy stored in the capacitor after the switch is closed compared with the energy stored in the capacitor before the switch is closed?

Key.Rationale: It would be impossible for the capacitor to gain energy in this scenario. The capacitor has to initially drive charge around the new loop through `R_2`, thus losing potential energy at the expense of energy lost through heat in the resistor.

In the initial state, there is no current at equilibrium and the potential difference across the fully charged capacitor is the entire battery potential. When the switch is closed, there will be current in both resistors, so there is a potential difference across `R_1`. Thus the new potential difference across the capacitor is less and `1/2CV^2` will have a lower value. Another way to think about it is that charge will be moved by the capacitor through the new “loop” created when `R_2` is included in the circuit. This will reduce the charge and the potential difference across the capacitor, thus reducing the energy.
There must be a loss of energy as the capacitor moves charge through the new loop.

D.Choice: The energy cannot be determined without knowing the resistances of the resistors.

Key.Rationale: The values of the resistors are not necessary to know that there was an energy change in the capacitor.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/46a.jpg

The figure above represents part of a student's experiment in which polar molecules are moving toward the top of the page at high speed. The molecules are modeled as atoms with a positive and a negative charge connected by a molecular bond. The molecules pass through a narrow region of uniform electric field directed to the right. Since the molecules have no net charge, the student expects that the field will have no effect on them and is puzzled to find that the molecules have a higher average energy when they emerge on the other side of the field. Which of the following could explain the student's observation? Select `text(two)` answers.

A.Choice: Since some molecules enter the field aligned at an angle to the field - like the molecule on the left - the field exerts a torque on them, which causes them to rotate and gives them rotational kinetic energy.

Key.Rationale: The electric field is directed to the right, therefore a to the right on the positive end, creating a torque and initiating clockwise rotation of the molecule. Likewise, the field exerts a force to the left on the negative end, also initiating a torque and clockwise rotation. This external torque on the molecule produces rotational kinetic energy, adding to the total kinetic energy of the molecule.

B.Choice: Since the molecules are polar, they behave as if they have a net charge. The field exerts a net force on them that does work and gives them linear kinetic energy.

Key.Rationale: The molecules do not have a net charge, even though they are polar.

C.Choice: Since some molecules enter the field aligned parallel to its direction - like the molecule in the middle - the field exerts forces in opposite directions on the `text(two)` atoms, which stretches the molecular bonds and gives the molecules internal energy.

Key.Rationale: Some molecules will enter the field aligned with the direction of the field, so the electric field exerts a force to the right on the positive end of the molecule and a force to the left on the negative end of the molecule (`F=qE`), stretching the molecular bonds and increasing internal energy of the molecules.

D.Choice: Since some molecules enter the field aligned perpendicular to its direction - like the molecule on the right - the field exerts forces in opposite directions on the `text(two)` atoms. The force on the positive charge is greater, so the net force does work and gives them linear kinetic energy.

Key.Rationale: Because the molecules have no net charge, the magnitude of charge on `text(each end)` of the polar molecules is the same. If the charges are the same, the force exerted on `text(each end)` is the same, i.e., equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.

A sample of an ideal gas can be taken from state `i` to state `f` via `text(two)` processes, as shown in the above graph of pressure `P` versus volume `V`. In `text(one)` process the gas goes through state `X`, and in the other process the gas goes through state `Y`. Which of the following will be the same for both processes? Select `text(two)` answers.

A.Choice: The change in the internal energy of the gas

Key.Rationale: The change in internal energy of the gas depends only on change in temperature (`DeltaUpropDeltaT`). The difference in temperature between point `i` and point `f` will be the same, regardless of path.

B.Choice: The temperature of the gas at the end of the process

Key.Rationale: Temperature at `text(each point)` depends on the pressure and volume at that point (`PV=nRT`). The temperature at point `f` will be determined by `P` and `V` at that point, not on the path during the process.

C.Choice: The thermal energy transferred to the gas by heating

Key.Rationale: The `text(first)` law of thermodynamics (energy conservation) internal energy is the sum of thermal energy gain and work done on the gas (`DeltaU=Q+W`). The process through point `X` has more work done by the gas (which is considered negative using the above equation) than the process through point `Y`. Because the change in internal energy is the same for both, more thermal energy must be added during the process through point `X`.

D.Choice: The work done on the gas

Key.Rationale: Regardless of sign convention used, work is calculated as process “curve” and the volume axis. It is clear that the area for the process through `X` is different than the area through process `Y`.

Identical samples of gas initially have pressure `P_0`, volume `V_0`, and temperature `T_0`. In some experiments, students take samples through each of the processes shown in the graph above. The final temperature is equal to the initial temperature for which of the processes? Select `text(two)` answers.

Key.Rationale: Use the ideal gas law, `PV=nRT`; therefore `T=PV//nR`. Because `n` and `R` are constant for these samples, we only need to examine the product `PV` in `text(each case)`. For process `A`, the initial product is `P_0V_0` and the final product is `(1//2P_0)(2V_0)`, so the products are equal and temperature does not change.
For process `B`, the initial product is `P_0V_0` and the final product is `(3P_0)(1.5V_0)`, so they are not equal and thus the temperature changes.

Use the ideal gas law, `PV=nRT`, so `T=PV//nR`. Because `n` and `R` are constant for these samples, we examine only the product `PV` in `text(each case)` to see if `T` is constant. For process `C`, the initial product is `P_0V_0` and the final product is `(1//3P_0)(1.5V_0)`, so the products are equal and temperature does not change.
For process `D`, the initial product is `P_0V_0` and the final product is `(1//3P_0)(1.5V_0)`, so they are not equal and therefore the temperature changes.

Content: A beam of electrons is moving at a speed of `6xx10^6` `text(m)//text(s)`. If the beam is incident on each of the following objects, for which of the objects will diffraction be observed? Select `text(two)` answers.

Key.Rationale: An electron at the speed given has a de Broglie wavelength `lambda=h//p` of `1.2xx10^-10`. The width of the human hair (on the order of `10^-5` `text(m)`) is too large (by too many orders of magnitude) to diffract electrons.

An electron moving at `6` `text(m)//text(s)` has a de Broglie wavelength (`lambda=h//p`) as calculated: `lambda=(6.63xx10^-34` `text(J)*text(s))//(9.11xx10^-31` `text(kg))(6xx10^6` `text(m)//text(s))=1.2xx10^-10` `text(m)`. The opening must be small (within several orders of magnitude of the wavelength). The width of the interatomic spacing in the crystal is close enough to the wavelength for interference diffraction to occur, as shown by the well known Davisson-Germer experiment.

An electron at the speed given has a de Broglie wavelength (`lambda=h//p`). Using the mass of an electron and Planck's constant: `lambda=(6.63xx10^-34` `text(J)*text(s))//(9.11xx10^-31` `text(kg))(6xx10^6` `text(m)//text(s))=1.2xx10^-10` `text(m)`. The opening must be small (within several orders of magnitude of the wavelength). The width of the slit is within about `text(one)` order of magnitude larger than the wavelength, so diffraction of electrons could occur.

An electron at the speed given has a de Broglie wavelength `lambda=h//p` of `1.2xx10^-10`. The width of the paper strip is too large (by too many orders of magnitude) for diffraction of electrons to occur.

Content: problems/AP14P2/media/50a.jpg

The graph above shows the maximum kinetic energy of electrons released in the photoelectric effect as a function of the frequency of the incident light. This graph is often used as evidence of the particle nature of light. The graph supports which of the following statements? Select `text(two)` answers.

A.Choice: The number of photoelectrons increases as the frequency increases.

Key.Rationale: As frequency increases, the energy of `text(each photon)` increases but not necessarily the number of photons.

B.Choice: There is a threshold frequency below which no photoemission occurs.

Key.Rationale: The maximum kinetic energy of electrons is equal to the energy of photons striking the metal (`E=hf`) minus the work function of the metal: `K_text(max)=hf-Phi`. When `K` is `text(zero)`, `hf=Phi` and the frequency is called the threshold frequency, below which no photoemission occurs. The threshold frequency is the `xtext(-intercept)` on this graph.

C.Choice: The energy of photoelectrons depends on the energy of the incoming light.

Key.Rationale: The maximum kinetic energy of electrons is equal to the energy of photons striking the metal (`E=hf`) minus the work function of the metal: `K_text(max)=hf-Phi`. When `K` is `text(zero)`, `hf=Phi` and the frequency is called the threshold frequency, below which no photoemission occurs. The threshold frequency is the `xtext(-intercept)` on this graph, and `K` increases as frequency increases beyond the threshold.

D.Choice: The intensity of the incoming light determines whether photoemission occurs.

Key.Rationale: Intensity of light is not a factor, as `text(each photon)` must have frequency above the threshold frequency to produce emission. This choice incorrectly assumes that increasing intensity, which increases total energy, will produce photoemission and does not consider the quantum effect.
